items.excerpt: The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, the first such finding against a state by that court. Presidents Trump, Xi and Putin issued a joint declaration after their first three-way meeting in Shenzhen. ... ### World Court rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority. It is the first time the court has held a state responsible for genocide. The vote was nine to six. The case, brought by The Gambia, concerns the 2017 military operation that killed thousands and drove hundreds of thousands into Bangladesh. The Gambia welcomed the ruling. More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced. Questions remain over how the judgment will be enforced. Why it matters: The ruling sets a legal precedent for genocide cases elsewhere and bears on more than 1.3 million displaced Rohingya. Myanmar's military launched an operation in Rakhine state in 2017 that sent hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fleeing to Bangladesh. The Gambia filed the case at the ICJ in 2019. Myanmar had denied genocide. ... ### Trump, Xi and Putin hold first three-way summit, issue peace declaration ... The leaders of the US, China and Russia met in Shenzhen on Thursday and signed a four-point joint declaration. It covers reducing nuclear risk, United Nations reform, energy supply stability and the International Criminal Court's jurisdiction. The text does not mention Ukraine or Iran. Trump called Putin a friend, which drew criticism from some world leaders. Analysts told outlets that no major breakthroughs came out of the roughly 70-minute talks. Why it matters: Europe and Ukraine were not at the table, and the talks touch nuclear arms and energy supply worldwide. The three leaders met on the sidelines of the APEC summit hosted by China. The US and Russia are in conflict over the war in Ukraine, and the US is also at war with Iran. ... ### Anthropic closes 17% above IPO price in Nasdaq debut Anthropic shares closed around $97 on their first day, 17% above the $83 offer price. The Claude chatbot maker opened at $111.50. The company raised $81.3 billion, a record for an initial public offering, at a valuation near $1.5 trillion. Three protesters were arrested outside the exchange. Analysts warned the shares may be volatile, and the debut did not revive a weak AI trade. Why it matters: It is the first listing of a pure AI company and a test of investor appetite for the sector. ... ### Ukraine's allies meet in Berlin, say Europe ready to talk with Russia Leaders of the coalition of the willing met in Berlin and said Europe has a united position for talks with Russia. US envoy Jared Kushner said Trump is open to a NATO-style security guarantee for Ukraine. Macron urged allies to reopen the question of Ukraine's NATO membership. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized the Shenzhen format. Trump reportedly told the leaders by phone that Putin wants to end the war. ... ### Houthi missile damages Saudi sovereign wealth fund tower in Riyadh Houthi missiles hit Riyadh's financial district, damaging the Public Investment Fund tower and other buildings. No injuries were reported.

items.title: AI is fueling "disturbingly high" inflation, Chicago Fed president says - CBS News
items.excerpt: The boom in AI data center construction is adding to the nation's "borderline disturbingly high" inflation, with the sector's massive business investment indirectly contributing to rising service prices, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday. "The AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy," Goolsbee said. "I find it hard to look at it any other way when you are getting major business investment, almost an unprecedented level of business investment." Goolsbee, who will become a voting member of the interest rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee in January, declined to forecast the central bank's next moves on interest rates. But he said the Fed's decisions will be determined by whether U.S. inflation is on track to return to the central bank's annual 2% target. "The evidence does not suggest we are on a path back to 2%," Goolsbee added.

items.title: Higher fuel prices seep into core inflation - Dallasfed.org
items.excerpt: Alexander Chudik, Lutz Kilian and Xiaoqing Zhou November 19, 2026 Fuel prices have been on a wild ride since late February 2026, when military strikes on Iran set off sharp moves in oil and fuel markets. Retail gasoline prices aside, the U.S. retail diesel price reached an all-time high, the jet fuel price is near its previous peak, and the heating oil price has set a new record. The U.S. price of natural gas, meanwhile, has barely budged. The fuel price surge has been very uneven. Diesel prices in particular moved sharply higher. Diesel is the fuel of the freight economy. Trucks, trains, ships and farm equipment run on it, which means its price may potentially touch the cost of moving nearly everything consumers buy. The price gap between diesel and gasoline has widened significantly in recent months. On Sept. 22, 2026, the national average retail price of diesel reached $6.53 per gallon, about 70 percent above its level at the end of February (compared with a 50 percent rise for retail gasoline). The diesel rise surpassed the fuel’s previous record set in 2022 (Chart 1). Prices have eased only modestly, to about $6.31 as of the end of October. Consumers experience these prices directly at the pump and indirectly on their utility bills. But fuel prices may also work their way into the prices of other goods and services, from airline tickets to paper towels. Economists call these "second-round effects," and they matter for the Federal Reserve because they show up in core inflation, an inflation measure that excludes food and energy. Policymakers watch core inflation closely to gauge underlying price pressures. Our estimates suggest that higher fuel prices added between 20 and 60 basis points to 12-month core inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, as of September 2026. If fuel prices simply held at their current levels, that contribution would gradually decline by about 30 basis points by the end of 2027.

items.title: Fed’s Jefferson says AI boosting inflation, productivity impact possible ’in the future’ By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The rapid artificial intelligence buildout is putting upward pressure on US inflation through its impact on demand, Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said on Thursday, with possible productivity gains that could help ease price pressures only coming "in the future." In prepared remarks to a Brazilian central bank conference, Jefferson said the AI boom is the sort of shock that could influence both demand and supply, but at different points in time. "On the demand side, optimism about the technology has been boosting business investment in data centers, advanced computing equipment, and related products," Jefferson said. "Currently, the AI buildout is exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation." Productivity improvements from the new technology could put downward pressure on prices, but only "in the future," Jefferson said, without estimating a timeline.

items.title: Fed minutes October 2026: Officials expect more rate hikes, worry about AI
items.excerpt: Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday. Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk." More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December. The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."

items.title: US Senate rejects bid to curb Trump's Iran war powers
items.excerpt: US Senate Republicans have rejected legislation directing Donald Trump to end the war in Iran or obtain Congress’ ‌approval to continue it, backing the President weeks after sweeping defeats ‌in midterm elections largely tied to Americans’ frustration with the conflict. The Senate voted 51 to 48 on Thursday, largely along party lines, to defeat a war powers resolution that had previously passed the House of ‌Representatives. Only three Republicans – ‌Susan ⁠Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and ​Rand Paul of Kentucky – voted with Democrats in favour of the resolution. One Democrat, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, voted with Republicans against it. The vote marked the first time the Senate had considered ⁠a major Iran war-related measure since ‌Democratic ​victories in the midterm elections on November 3. Trump’s fellow Republicans, ​who rarely break ‌with the President, stood behind him in support of the ​US-Israel war on Iran that started on February 28. Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia, who has called repeatedly ​for ​Congress to take back ​its control over declarations of war, said ‌the midterm election result reflected Americans’ unhappiness about the war, and higher prices for food, fuel and other goods linked to the conflict. “Its unpopularity was made absolutely, manifestly clear in the ​election results of November 3,” Kaine said in a ​speech before the vote ⁠appealing for yes votes. Meanwhile, the costs of the Iran war have risen to an estimated $US48.3 billion ($A72.3 billion) as of November 13, but because that total does not include damage to US bases attacked in the Middle East, lawmakers are pushing for the Pentagon to provide those figures. Arthur Miller, a Pentagon budget official, provided the latest overall cost estimate on Thursday to the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering his nomination to be Navy comptroller. The $US48 billion ($A72 billion) figure includes the costs of military operations, as well as for replacing equipment and munitions. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut pressed Miller for an estimate on damage to US installations, which Miller said he didn’t have. Republican Senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the committee’s chair, directed Miller to try to provide an answer as soon as possible.

The 13-track album, released on July 31, 2026, has been nominated for Best Global Music Album at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards. Its mix of international collaborators reflects Afrobeats’ continued reach across borders, with the two South Africans among those credited on the project. ... ## 9. Beyoncé reaches 100 Grammy nominations Beyoncé has added another historic milestone to an already record-breaking Grammy career, becoming the first artist to reach 100 nominations. Her latest recognition comes for Morning Dew (Donk), which has been nominated for Best R&B Solo Performance at the 2027 Grammy Awards. The song was released in July ahead of the 20th anniversary of her album “B’Day”. The milestone adds to a career that began collecting Grammy recognition with Destiny’s Child in 2000, when the group earned nominations for “Bills, Bills, Bills”. Beyoncé remains the most-awarded artist in Grammy history with 35 wins.

items.title: 'GTA 6' Soundtrack & Gracie Abrams Lead Best New Music: Friday Guide
items.excerpt: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album The video game that defined a generation is back with a new edition — and a star-studded soundtrack to boot. Featuring contributions from Dua Lipa, Cardi B, Morgan Wallen, Tame Impala, King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard, SZA, Travis Scott, Justice, JENNIE, Lana Del Rey, Zara Larsson and Rauw Alejandro, Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album translates the game’s high-octane, gun-toting world into music spanning hip-hop, dance, Latin, country and more. Even though 10 tracks were released ahead of the full album, this towering compilation has more than enough new material for both gamers and casual listeners to sink their teeth into. — KYLE DENIS Gracie Abrams, “Lost In It” Four months after releasing her third album, Daughter From Hell, the pop singer is sharing its deluxe with five new tracks. Abrams already dropped the more experimentally-produced single “Here You Come, There You Go,” which she performed as musical guest on Saturday Night Live and is co-written and co-produced by Jim-E Stack. Stack is also credited on new focus track “Lost In It” and “Out Of Nowhere” — both of which are more uptempo — while longtime collaborator Aaron Dessner is credited on “Crazy Girl” and “Love Letter,” both of which feature his signature layered and intimate production. — LYNDSEY HAVENS LISA, “Leave With Me” “Spread my wings, fly / me on my side,” sings LISA on the melodic ballad “Leave With Me,” which is featured over the end credits of her new YouTube Premium movie Always Lalisa. Its release coincides with the kick-off of VIVA LA LISA, the first Vegas residency from a K-pop artist. Fittingly, “Leave With Me” chronicles the feeling of quite literally flying solo — and the song and LISA’s journey so far proves, she’s not just flying but soaring on her own. ... TOMORROW X TOGETHER, “Angel Bite” This week, South Korean boy band TXT released its ninth mini album. Perfect Storm includes six songs, including electro-pop focus track “Angel Bite” that continues the group’s distinct deliver of love songs. ... Yet, the group will soon face the familiar as it heads on its fifth world tour across North America and Europe in 2027. ... beabadoobee, “No Punctuation” Indie-pop artist beabadoobee is on a roll — luckily for us. Having just released her fourth album this year, in September, she has now announced her fifth album will arrive in February.
